title: A Grip Switched On From Inside

scenes.tts: A white blood cell is carried along in flowing blood, and it must stop where it is needed. There, it can stop on the vessel wall in about a second. What switches its grip on? A second is too short to make a new protein. So the receptor that grips must already sit on the cell surface, switched off.
scenes.visual: A cell slides along a vessel wall in flowing blood and halts at a marked spot while a clock sweeps one second. A question mark sits at the contact. A crossed-out new-protein box rules out building a grip, and dim dots on the cell edge show a grip that is already there and switched off.
scenes.narration: A white blood cell is carried along in flowing blood, and it must stop where it is needed. There, it can stop on the vessel wall in about a second. What switches its grip on? A second is too short to make a new protein. So the receptor that grips must already sit on the cell surface, switched off.

scenes.tts: The receptor that grips the wall is an integrin. It is two different chains, called alpha and beta, and each chain crosses the membrane once. Their large outer parts together form a head that grips its ligand. Inside the cell, each chain has only a short tail. There is no kinase domain and no channel.
scenes.caption: The receptor that grips the wall is an integrin. It is two different chains, called α and β, and each chain crosses the membrane once. Their large outer parts together form a head that grips its ligand. Inside the cell, each chain has only a short tail. There is no kinase domain and no channel.
scenes.visual: The cell edge zooms into a flat membrane. Two chains grow up through it and meet in a cup-shaped head, a ligand hangs from the wall above, and two short tails reach down inside. Crossed-out kinase and channel boxes show what the integrin lacks.
scenes.narration: The receptor that grips the wall is an integrin. It is two different chains, called α and β, and each chain crosses the membrane once. Their large outer parts together form a head that grips its ligand. Inside the cell, each chain has only a short tail. There is no kinase domain and no channel.

scenes.tts: In integrins studied most closely, those of platelets and white blood cells, the outer part can fold at a knee. The head then tips back toward the membrane. Bent, with the head closed, the integrin holds its ligand weakly. A white blood cell flowing in the blood keeps its integrins in this form. So the grip is switched off.
scenes.visual: The legs fold at the knee, the head tips back and its cup closes, and the ligand is left hanging above, joined by a thin dashed thread. A switch labelled grip shows off and the cell is shown flowing.
scenes.narration: In integrins studied most closely, those of platelets and white blood cells, the outer part can fold at a knee. The head then tips back toward the membrane. Bent, with the head closed, the integrin holds its ligand weakly. A white blood cell flowing in the blood keeps its integrins in this form. So the grip is switched off.

scenes.tts: A signal on the vessel wall starts a relay inside the cell. The relay helps bring a protein called talin to the integrin tail. Talin binds the tail of the beta chain and separates the two tails. The change passes through the membrane, the outer part straightens, and the head opens. Extended like this, the integrin holds its ligand tightly.
scenes.caption: A signal on the vessel wall starts a relay inside the cell. The relay helps bring a protein called talin to the integrin tail. Talin binds the tail of the β chain and separates the two tails. The change passes through the membrane, the outer part straightens, and the head opens. Extended like this, the integrin holds its ligand tightly.
scenes.visual: A signal on the wall sends an arrow into the cell to a relay and on to talin. Talin docks on the beta tail, the tails swing apart, a pulse runs up through the membrane, the knee straightens and the cup opens. The grip switch flips on.
scenes.narration: A signal on the vessel wall starts a relay inside the cell. The relay helps bring a protein called talin to the integrin tail. Talin binds the tail of the β chain and separates the two tails. The change passes through the membrane, the outer part straightens, and the head opens. Extended like this, the integrin holds its ligand tightly.

scenes.tts: The extended integrin grabs its ligand on the vessel wall and holds it tightly. The cell stops. Nothing had to be made, so the relay can run in about a second. The message started inside the cell and changed the grip outside. So this is called inside-out signalling.
scenes.visual: The ligand drops into the open cup and the head glows green; the cell status changes from flowing to stopped. A crossed-out new-protein box and a clock sweeping one second sit by the relay. An arrow runs from the tails up to the head, labelled inside-out.
scenes.narration: The extended integrin grabs its ligand on the vessel wall and holds it tightly. The cell stops. Nothing had to be made, so the relay can run in about a second. The message started inside the cell and changed the grip outside. So this is called inside-out signalling.

scenes.tts: A hormone receptor waits for its ligand. An integrin is often surrounded by ligand, so the cell controls the receptor instead. So ligand can be all around, and the cell can still keep the grip weak. The control is a change of shape, thrown from inside the cell. Keep this rule: signals inside the cell can strengthen an integrin's grip.
scenes.visual: Two panels. Left: a hormone receptor with an empty cup waits until a ligand arrives. Right: a bent integrin among many ligands stays off until talin arrives from inside, and the legs straighten and the head opens so one ligand is held. The labels read: the ligand decides, the cell decides.
scenes.narration: A hormone receptor waits for its ligand. An integrin is often surrounded by ligand, so the cell controls the receptor instead. So ligand can be all around, and the cell can still keep the grip weak. The control is a change of shape, thrown from inside the cell. Keep this rule: signals inside the cell can strengthen an integrin's grip.
